Name: The Naval Legacy of the Corvus Boarding Bridge and the Close Fighting of Rams
RagShortTexts: In the First Punic War Rome invented the corvus boarding bridge, forcibly turning naval battle into hand-to-hand fighting on deck
In the Second Punic War the bridge was abandoned because it risked sinking ships in rough seas, and Rome returned to ramming tactics handled by sailors
The bronze ram of a quinquereme struck at full speed to tear open the waterline and keel of an enemy ship
BaseText: The mechanics of naval warfare went through a dramatic evolution over the two Punic Wars. In the First Punic War, the Romans, inexperienced at sea, invented the 'raven' boarding bridge (Corvus): a rotating bridge was mounted upright on the bow of a warship, with a heavy iron beak at its end. When it struck an enemy ship, the iron beak smashed through the enemy deck and locked it fast, and Roman heavy infantry then swarmed across to fight hand to hand. But the tall bridge raised the ship's center of gravity too high, and in storms it caused several mass capsizings and sinkings of hundreds of Roman warships. By the Second Punic War, Rome had abandoned the corvus completely and relied instead on well-trained sailors, sturdy hulls and the heavy bronze three-pronged ram (Ram/Rostra) below the waterline. The focus of naval battle returned to the classic close-fighting mechanics of the ram: full-speed broadside impacts that tore open keels, and sweeping strokes that sheared off an enemy ship's oars and left it crippled.

Variants.Content: Even without the corvus, Roman warriors are invincible once their feet touch the sea! The moment the ram bites through the enemy keel is the moment the short sword reaps enemy heads.

The sea belongs to true sailors again! Without those clumsy wooden bridges getting in the way, with the light turning of our quinqueremes and our skilled rowers we can leave the Romans behind in wind and waves.

The bronze ram cast on the bow weighs hundreds of pounds, and the impact of a full-speed charge is enough to snap a trireme in two at the waist. Naval battle has always been a brutal contest of wood, stone and metal.
